challenges.name: Array Streak
challenges.note: Nine correct actions in a row

hazards.battery-terminal: Those are the battery terminals. A DC battery bank has no zero-crossing: a spanner across them vaporises and takes your hand with it.
hazards.damaged-conduit: That conduit is crushed and the conductors inside are chafed. Energising a damaged run puts fault current into the roof structure.
hazards.hot-mc4: You pulled an MC4 under load. A live DC string will not stop arcing when the plug separates — the array is a current source for as long as the sun is on it.
hazards.roof-edge: You walked to an unprotected edge with no anchor. Falls from height are the single largest killer in this trade and the roof does not care how experienced you are.
hazards.skylight: That is a skylight, not a step. A domed acrylic light on an unscreened curb carries no weight at all — people go through them every year and land on a floor two storeys down, and from above a dirty skylight on a ballasted roof looks like part of the deck. It gets a screen or a guardrail before anybody works within falling distance of it.

interrupts.alert: The inverter display has lit and the module glass has come back up behind you. Somebody has put AC back on the board downstairs and the rapid shutdown has reset.
interrupts.cue: The conductors under your feet are at full string voltage again.
interrupts.missNote: You went on metering a string that had come back to six hundred volts DC. A PV array is a current source with no zero crossing: the first thing that tells you the conductors are live is the arc, and the reflex that follows an arc on a roof puts you somewhere you did not choose to be.
interrupts.why: Rapid shutdown is a state that has to be held, not an action that stays done. The transmitter needs power to keep telling the module-level devices to stay open, so the moment somebody restores the board below you the array closes back in at full open-circuit voltage. None of that touches your disconnects — they are still open and still locked, and that is precisely why an open disconnect is not what makes a roof safe while the sun is up. The initiator goes back in before a lead is touched.
interrupts.wrongNote: That is not what brings the array down. The initiator is at the roof access, and it goes in again before anything else happens up here.

interrupts.alert: Your lanyard is lying slack across the deck. The hook has come off the anchor eye as you worked along the array and you are attached to nothing.
interrupts.cue: You are three paces from an edge with no parapet.
interrupts.missNote: You finished the string tests unattached, on a deck with one unprotected edge and no parapet along it. Nothing pulled you over, and that is the only reason this is a note rather than a fatality — the protection was simply absent for the whole of that step and you had no idea.
interrupts.why: Fall protection fails quietly. A karabiner rolled out against the lip of an anchor eye, a gate nudged open by a module frame, a line paid out past the distance it was rigged for — none of it makes a sound, and every one of them leaves a person working exactly as confidently as they were a minute earlier. The connection is something you check by looking at it, not by feeling the weight of the line, and the work stops the second it is in question rather than at the end of the test you were part way through.
interrupts.wrongNote: That is not what you are attached to. Get back on the certified anchor before you take another reading.

lateNotes.bess-panel: The battery comes last — the array side is isolated first so you are not working two live sources at once.
lateNotes.string-meter: Nothing gets metered until the array is in rapid shutdown and both disconnects are open.

steps.cue: Read the plan: anchor points, edge distances, array layout.
steps.prompt: Read the plan: anchor points, edge distances, array layout.
steps.title: Survey the roof and anchor plan
steps.why: Falls from height are the single largest killer in this trade, which is exactly what OSHA 29 CFR 1926.501 exists to answer: a duty to have fall protection wherever the exposure is, decided before anybody is exposed to it. You establish where the certified anchors are, where the unprotected edge runs and where the skylights sit before you ever step onto the deck — not while you are already standing three paces from one of them.

steps.cue: Clip the lifeline to the certified anchor and put your weight on it — hold the load until the connection has proved itself.
steps.holdBreakNote: You came off the connection before it had taken any real load. A pull test that stops the moment it starts to feel like effort has proved nothing about the base plate under that anchor.
steps.prompt: Clip the lifeline to the certified anchor and put your weight on it — hold the load until the connection has proved itself.
steps.title: Rig the anchor and proof the connection
steps.why: The anchor is rated to 22 kN and inspected on the schedule ANSI Z359, the Fall Protection Code, sets out, and the certified eye is the only thing on this roof that carries that rating. Connecting to a vent stack or a conduit run instead because it happens to be closer is exactly how an anchorage fails at the one moment its rating is actually asked for, and pulling steadily against the connection now is how you find a loose base plate or a rolled-out gate while a fall is still hypothetical.

steps.cue: Go over the harness before it goes on — four things, and the hints will not point at them.

decoyNotes.spare-harness: That is the spare in the chest, and its inspection tag is last year's. A harness whose tag is out of date does not get worn while you work out whether it is probably fine — it goes out of service.

itemNotes.harness: Webbing run through your hands a span at a time — no cuts, no fraying, no glazed or hardened patch where it has been near heat.
itemNotes.harness-absorber: The energy absorber's cover is intact and its warning flag is unbroken, so this lanyard has never taken a fall.
itemNotes.harness-dring: The dorsal D-ring sits flat and square with no pitting, no elongation and no hairline crack across the bend.
itemNotes.harness-hook: The snap hook closes fully, the gate springs shut on its own and the locking sleeve engages without being helped.

steps.prompt: Go over the harness before it goes on — four things, and the hints will not point at them.
steps.title: Inspect and don the harness
steps.why: A harness is inspected at every single use, not on a calendar, because everything that takes it out of service happens between uses: a cut from a panel frame, a glazed patch from a hot roof, a D-ring pitted by grit, an absorber whose flag has been pulled. Every one of those passes a casual glance and every one of them passes right up until the single fall the harness is finally asked to arrest, which is the first and last time it will ever be tested.

steps.cue: Hit the rapid shutdown initiator at the roof access.
steps.prompt: Hit the rapid shutdown initiator at the roof access.
steps.title: Initiate rapid shutdown
steps.why: Rapid shutdown drops the array conductors outside the modules to a safe touch voltage within seconds of the initiator being pressed. It is the rapid-shutdown requirement that makes rooftop PV wiring approachable in daylight at all — without it, an array under sun is simply a live circuit.

steps.cue: Grab the DC disconnect handle and pull it open.
steps.prompt: Grab the DC disconnect handle and pull it open.
steps.title: Open the DC disconnect
steps.why: DC first, always. Opening the AC side while DC is still feeding the inverter leaves stored energy and a live front end sitting behind the cover you are about to work near — the inverter has to lose its source before it loses its grid connection.

steps.cue: Grab the AC disconnect handle and pull it open.
steps.prompt: Grab the AC disconnect handle and pull it open.
steps.title: Open the AC disconnect
steps.why: Now the inverter has neither a DC source feeding it nor a grid connection to push back into. Both sides open, in that order, is what makes the equipment actually isolated for electrical safe work purposes under NFPA 70E, rather than just sitting quiet.

steps.cue: Lock and tag the DC and AC disconnects.
steps.prompt: Lock and tag the DC and AC disconnects.
steps.title: Lock both disconnects
steps.why: Two isolations, two locks, because either one alone leaves a path back to a live conductor, and that is the whole point of OSHA 29 CFR 1910.147: the energy is controlled by a device only you can remove. An IBEW crew treats an inverter that gets reset remotely mid-string-test as a near miss rather than an inconvenience — the locks are what stop somebody downstairs from making that decision on your behalf.

steps.cue: Read Voc on string 3 and commit inside the expected band.

gauge.label: STRING 3 — OPEN CIRCUIT VOLTAGE
gauge.missNote: Off the expected Voc for this string. That is a module count or a connection problem — find it before commissioning.

steps.prompt: Read Voc on string 3 and commit inside the expected band.
steps.title: Measure string open-circuit voltage
steps.why: Measuring Voc against the expected value for this string's module count, wiring and temperature is how you find a missing module, a reversed pair or a shaded run before you ever energise — after commissioning, the same fault just looks like reduced output nobody can explain.

steps.cue: Polarity, then insulation resistance, then earth continuity.
steps.outOfOrderNote: Wrong order — polarity is confirmed before any test that injects voltage into the string.
steps.prompt: Polarity, then insulation resistance, then earth continuity.
steps.title: Complete the string tests in order
steps.why: Polarity first, because an insulation test on a reversed string tells you nothing useful and can damage the tester by driving current the wrong way through it. Earth continuity comes last because it confirms the protective bonding path every reading before it has been quietly relying on.

steps.cue: Read pack state of charge and commit inside the commissioning window.

gauge.label: PACK STATE OF CHARGE
gauge.missNote: Outside the commissioning window — bring the pack into range before the first cycle.

steps.prompt: Read pack state of charge and commit inside the commissioning window.
steps.title: Check the battery state
steps.why: A battery commissioned at the extremes of its charge window — nearly empty or nearly full — cannot be balanced properly across its cells, and the first charge cycle is exactly when that imbalance shows up as one cell ageing faster than the other five.

steps.cue: Remove the locks, energise in reverse order and log the commissioning data.
steps.prompt: Remove the locks, energise in reverse order and log the commissioning data.
steps.title: Energise and record
steps.why: Energise AC then DC — the exact reverse of how you isolated — watch the inverter come up clean, and record every reading you took. The commissioning record is what the next technician inherits instead of guessing at this array's baseline from scratch.
